I've been meaning to try mason jar preps. Have you found since you used them that you prefer them? Right now I'm using these and I like them pretty well except when it comes to cleaning.

TBH this is my first time ever using the mason jars. My usual containers are more similar to the ones you use, and I love them. Whenever my meal prep calls for salad though, I'm going to go with the mason jars. It really keeps the salad fresh and crisp, even the tomatoes and cucumbers!
How long can salads last in a mason jar? I would love to make arugula salads ahead of time, but the arugula always seems to start going bad in a few days.

Of the salads I made, I ate my last one on Day 10. The lettuce, peppers, and spinach were all still crisp and fresh. The cucumbers had begun to get a little soggy. As a general rule, most people don't recommend to leave them in the jar for longer than a week, but honestly I was fine with it. My biggest surprise was that the spinach held up so long and so nicely.

Follow up questions:

US expats: where did you relocate and why?

Nicaragua- the surfing is better than anywhere else on the planet and the people are amazing. Hawaii is OK as well, but too expensive.

When? Recently.

Challenges? Spanish and getting a car.

Again? In a heart beat.

what do you do for work over there? is it just "work enough to live" by being a busboy or something, or do you have a career that allows you to travel/work remotely?

Kudos to you for taking the leap :)

Right now just living cheap off savings. Hope to start a casino soon. We're going to turn Nicaragua into the next Macau and take all the money the Chinese made from American consumers back. It's the great circle of capitalist life. :)

I know next to nothing about Nicaragua, but according to Wikipedia it is one of the poorest countries in the Americas. Has it been easy adjusting? Do you still have a lot of the comforts of the States? Anything you miss? Thanks for the response!

It's true that my family struggled at first to adjust to the different world view. However, it is a different world and comparing the two ways of living is difficult. So called 1st world countries are dedicated to the accumulation of wealth for the sake of wealth. People in those countries spend most of their waking hours dedicated to the accumulation of more and more things for the sake of having more and more things- but few spend much time actually enjoying the accumulation when they have it. Nicaragua is truly a different world view. Wealth is great and all, but very few Nicas spend much time worrying about it. Building strong families and meaningful community relationships is the priority here. Nicas are a very proud people and they consider repairing old and worn out clothes or items a matter of honor, even when they could buy new things. As to creature comforts, there's a few things like automatically trusting a public drinking fountain, but we adapt and make do with bottled water. Mostly, I don't miss the constant competition to keep up with my neighbors shiny new toys. Here you enjoy what you have and if you don't enjoy it, then you don't keep it. You can get anything from the states here, if you are willing to pay for it. But really, going native is the way to go. In the states most people spend a lot of money eating out many times a month. You can do that here to, but it is easier to just eat the same thing every day. A neighborhood guy walks past every morning and delivers fresh frijoles, another neighbor brings by fresh tortillas, another fresh rice. We can feed our family for a few bucks a day, eat like the locals, and have an amazing time.

After the change in world view the adjustment was easy. However, not being a native Spanish speaker is hard. However, in SJDS there is a large expat community so most people speak English around here. Other parts of the country, it would be more difficult.
Thank you for such a thorough reply! I never thought about it that way. My reasons for emigrating would be to escape the ever expanding corporatism of the US.
